```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)
```

What do the symbols mean, and where do the numbers come from? Every chapter of
this book manipulates the same handful of objects, a matrix of returns, a vector
of weights, a mean vector and a covariance matrix, and @markowitz1952 needed all
four before he could state the problem the rest of the book solves. Following
@coqueret2020 and @scheuch2023, whose books open the same way, we fix the
notation once here so that no later chapter redefines a symbol, and we describe
the two sources of data once so that no later chapter has to explain what it is
computing on.

We first fix the notation and the conventions for annualizing, then describe the
modeled market on which every chapter runs, its calendar and the choices that
went into building it, then the real-data layer the book reaches for when a claim has to
be about real markets, and finally the vocabulary that maps the names in the data
onto the names the industry uses. This chapter sits on neither side of the
strategic–tactical distinction that @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory
defines; it is the ground both stand on.

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(xts)
library(PortfolioAnalytics)
library(PerformanceAnalytics)
library(tidypm)
```

## Notation {#sec-02-notation-and-data-notation}

Vectors are bold lower case, matrices are bold capitals, and a prime denotes the
transpose. There are $N$ assets observed over $T$ periods. The object everything
else is computed from is the $T \times N$ matrix of simple returns
$\boldsymbol{R}$, whose element $r_{t,i}$ is the return on asset $i$ over period
$t$,

$$
r_{t,i} = \frac{P_{t,i} + D_{t,i}}{P_{t-1,i}} - 1,
$$ {#eq-02-simple-return}

with $P$ the price and $D$ whatever the asset paid out during the period, so that
every return in this book is a total return. Simple returns rather than log
returns, because a portfolio's simple return is the weighted average of its
constituents' simple returns and that linearity is what makes @eq-02-moments
below true; log returns aggregate over time and not across assets, and the
book aggregates across assets far more often.

The risk-free rate over period $t$ is $r_{f,t}$, the return on a Treasury bill
bought at the start of the period and held to its end, and it is the only return
in the book that is known at the start of the period it applies to. **Excess
returns, $r_{t,i} - r_{f,t}$, are the default basis throughout.** Every mean,
covariance, Sharpe ratio and optimizer input is computed on excess returns
unless a chapter says otherwise, and the risk-free asset enters an optimization
as the origin of the return axis rather than as a column of the return matrix.
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory argues why: a constant column makes
the covariance matrix singular, a tangency portfolio exists only relative to a
risk-free rate in the sense of @tobin1958, and only the excess formulation stays
coherent when weights are allowed to sum to less than one. Here we only state
the convention.

The portfolio is the vector $\boldsymbol{w} \in \mathbb{R}^N$ of weights, one
per asset, and $\boldsymbol{\iota}$ is the vector of $N$ ones, so that
$\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1$ says the portfolio is fully invested.
The vector of expected excess returns is $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and the covariance
matrix of excess returns is $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. Both are population
quantities; an estimate of either carries a hat,
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, and the distinction
matters more in this book than in most, because Part III is about the gap
between the two. The portfolio's expected excess return and variance are

$$
\mu_{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu},
\qquad
\sigma^2_{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w},
$$ {#eq-02-moments}

and their ratio $\mu_{\boldsymbol{w}} / \sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}$ is the Sharpe
ratio of @sharpe1966, which on the excess basis needs no rate subtracted from
it. @sec-09-mean-variance-theory takes @eq-02-moments as its starting point.

### Annualizing

Returns arrive monthly and are reported annually, and the book uses two
conventions for the conversion, each in its place. Under the first, a monthly
mean is multiplied by twelve and a monthly standard deviation by $\sqrt{12}$, so
that a monthly Sharpe ratio is multiplied by $\sqrt{12}$; this is exact for the
mean and for the variance when returns are uncorrelated over time, and
@lo2002 gives the correction when they are not. It is the convention for
anything that enters or leaves an optimizer, because $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ are arithmetic objects. Under the second, the annual
return over a sample of $T$ months is the compounded one,

$$
\bar{r}_{\text{ann}} = \Big(\prod_{t=1}^{T}(1 + r_t)\Big)^{12/T} - 1,
$$ {#eq-02-compounded}

which is what an investor who held the series actually earned per year. It is
the convention for any table describing what a series did over the sample, and
for cumulative returns over an episode. Per period the compounded mean falls
short of the arithmetic one by roughly half the variance, and on a volatile
series that gap is not a rounding artifact: it is the variance drag, and
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation returns to it. We say which convention a
number follows wherever it could matter.

| Symbol | Meaning | Code |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $N$, $T$ | number of assets, number of periods | `ncol(R)`, `nrow(R)` |
| $t$ | a period, dated on the model calendar of @sec-02-notation-and-data-model-calendar | `zoo::index(R)`, `model_year()` |
| $\boldsymbol{R}$ | $T \times N$ matrix of simple total returns | `R` (an `xts`) |
| $r_{f,t}$ | risk-free rate over period $t$, the bill | `rf` |
| $\boldsymbol{R} - r_f\boldsymbol{\iota}'$ | excess returns, the default basis | `Re` |
| $\boldsymbol{w}$ | vector of portfolio weights | `w` |
| $\boldsymbol{\iota}$ | vector of $N$ ones | `rep(1, N)` |
| $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ | expected excess returns, and their estimate | `mu` |
| $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ | covariance matrix of excess returns, and its estimate | `S` |
| $\mu_{\boldsymbol{w}}$, $\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}$ | portfolio expected excess return and volatility | `p_ret(w)`, `p_vol(w)` |
| $\rho_{ij}$, $\sigma_{ij}$ | correlation and covariance of assets $i$ and $j$ | `cor(R)[i, j]`, `S[i, j]` |
| $\bar{r}_{\text{ann}}$ | compounded annual return, @eq-02-compounded | `ann_ret(x)` |

: Symbols used throughout the book, and the names the code gives them. {#tbl-02-symbols}

The right-hand column of @tbl-02-symbols is a convention too. Every chapter's
first code block builds the same three objects and nothing else, because
universe decisions are taken once, at import, and the excess-return basis is
argued once, in chapter 3. A reader who has seen the block below has seen every
data-preparation step the book performs:

```{r}
#| label: data
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # total returns
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess returns
stopifnot(ncol(R) == 16L, nrow(R) == length(rf), !anyNA(R))
```

`as_xts_pm()` is the boundary between the tidy world, where the data are stored
one row per asset per date in the sense of @wickham2023, and the wide `xts`
matrix `PortfolioAnalytics` requires; @sec-01-setting-up-implementation
explains the crossing and the three ways it fails. The `stopifnot()` is the
book's habit rather than decoration: wherever two objects must line up and
nothing in the language enforces it, the invariant is stated in code, so that a
mismatch fails the render rather than producing a plausible number.

As code, the two conventions are two lines, and every table in the book uses
them:

```{r}
#| label: conventions
ann_ret <- function(x, p = 12) prod(1 + x)^(p / length(x)) - 1   # compounded
ann_vol <- function(x, p = 12) stats::sd(x) * sqrt(p)             # sqrt-of-time
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: annualizing one series three ways

Take `US_equity`. Its monthly sample mean and standard deviation are

```{r}
#| label: worked-inputs
x   <- as.numeric(R[, "US_equity"])
m   <- mean(x)
s   <- stats::sd(x)
g   <- prod(1 + x)^(1 / length(x)) - 1          # compounded monthly mean
round(c(monthly_mean = m, monthly_sd = s, months = length(x)), 5)
```

so the arithmetic annual mean is $12 \times `r sprintf("%.5f", m)` =
`r sprintf("%.4f", 12 * m)`$, the annual volatility is
$\sqrt{12} \times `r sprintf("%.5f", s)` = `r sprintf("%.4f", s * sqrt(12))`$,
and the compounded return of @eq-02-compounded is

$$
\bar{r}_{\text{ann}}
= \Big(\prod_{t=1}^{`r length(x)`}(1 + r_t)\Big)^{12/`r length(x)`} - 1
= `r sprintf("%.4f", prod(1 + x))`^{\,`r sprintf("%.5f", 12 / length(x))`} - 1
= `r sprintf("%.4f", ann_ret(x))` .
$$

Per month, the arithmetic mean exceeds the compounded mean,
$`r sprintf("%.4f", prod(1 + x))`^{\,1/`r length(x)`} - 1 = `r sprintf("%.5f", g)`$,
by `r sprintf("%.5f", m - g)`, which is half the monthly variance,
$\tfrac{1}{2} \times `r sprintf("%.5f", s)`^2 = `r sprintf("%.5f", 0.5 * s^2)`$.
That is the variance drag. Between the two annual figures the gap is smaller,
`r sprintf("%.4f", 12 * m - ann_ret(x))` against half the annual variance of
`r sprintf("%.4f", 0.5 * (s * sqrt(12))^2)`, because the compounded figure also
earns return on return within the year,
`r sprintf("%.4f", (1 + g)^12 - 1 - 12 * g)`, and twelve times a monthly mean
does not. The same arithmetic in code:

```{r}
#| label: worked-check
round(c(arithmetic = 12 * m, compounded = ann_ret(x), volatility = ann_vol(x),
        monthly_gap = m - g, half_monthly_variance = 0.5 * s^2,
        annual_gap = 12 * m - ann_ret(x), half_annual_variance = 0.5 * ann_vol(x)^2,
        return_on_return = (1 + g)^12 - 1 - 12 * g), 5)
```
:::

## The Modeled Market {#sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market}

The default data of this book is a modeled market, and it contains no real
data. Factor models for government bonds, credit, equities and commodities were
estimated by historical simulation on market data from 1992 to 2022; the
factors were replayed, the idiosyncratic components drawn afresh, and the asset
paths reassembled, so that no series is the history of a real security. The
market therefore runs on its own calendar, model years
`r min(model_year(zoo::index(R)))` to `r max(model_year(zoo::index(R)))`. Its
stress episodes are named for what happens in them and ship as the table
`sim_episodes`. And because every series is the output of a factor model, the
market can be re-run with its factors shocked, which a history cannot, and
@sec-965-scenario-analysis does so.

Because it contains no real data, the whole market ships inside `tidypm` and
every number in this book reproduces offline, for every reader. The risk-free
rate, a three-month Treasury bill, and the exchange rates enter the model as
inputs. What the estimation on market data buys is realism of structure: the
stress episodes arrive in the right places and with the right relative
magnitudes, which @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application relies on.

### The model calendar {#sec-02-notation-and-data-model-calendar}

Because the data are modeled rather than recorded, a date in this market is a
position on the model's own calendar, not a point in history. The dates are
stored as ordinary `Date` objects, so that `xts` needs no special cases, but
their years are not calendar years. Four tools translate them, the same four in
every chapter: `model_year()` and `in_episode()` from `tidypm`, and
`fmt_model()` and `scale_x_model()` from the book's setup script,
`R/_common.R`.

`model_year()` turns a date into its model year, and `fmt_model()` writes a
date the way the prose does:

```{r}
#| label: calendar-years
d <- zoo::index(R)                                   # the month ends of the sample
range(d)                                             # as stored
range(model_year(d))                                 # as read
fmt_model(range(d))                                  # as written
worst <- d[which.min(as.numeric(R[, "US_equity"]))]  # a position is derived, never typed
fmt_model(worst)
```

The sample is thus `r nrow(R)` months, model years `r min(model_year(d))` to
`r max(model_year(d))`, and a point in it is named the way the worst month of
`US_equity` is: `r fmt_model(worst)`, or simply
`r fmt_model(worst, month = FALSE)`. The stress episodes are the rows of
`sim_episodes`, shown in @tbl-02-episodes, and the text calls each by its
label.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-02-episodes
#| tbl-cap: "The four named episodes of the modeled market, as shipped in `sim_episodes`. The key is what `in_episode()` takes; the label is what the text uses."
#| echo: false
sim_episodes |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    key    = paste0("`", episode, "`"),
    years  = ifelse(model_year(start) == model_year(end),
                    as.character(model_year(start)),
                    paste(model_year(start), "to", model_year(end))),
    months = vapply(episode, function(e) sum(in_episode(d, e)), integer(1))
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(key, label, years, months, description) |>
  kable(align = "llrrl",
        col.names = c("key", "label", "model years", "months", "description"))
```

`in_episode()` returns a logical vector that is `TRUE` on the dates of one
episode, so that no chapter types a window:

```{r}
#| label: calendar-episode
crisis <- in_episode(d, "credit_crisis")
in_crisis <- c(US_equity     = prod(1 + R[crisis, "US_equity"]) - 1,
               US_government = prod(1 + R[crisis, "US_government"]) - 1)
stopifnot(in_crisis[["US_equity"]] < 0, in_crisis[["US_government"]] > 0)
c(months = sum(crisis), round(in_crisis, 3))
```

Over the `r sum(crisis)` months of the credit crisis `US_equity` loses
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", -100 * in_crisis[["US_equity"]])` and `US_government`
gains `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * in_crisis[["US_government"]])`. On a time
axis, `scale_x_model()` takes the place of the date scale and labels model
years, as in @fig-02-calendar.

```{r}
#| label: fig-02-calendar
#| fig-cap: "The total-return index of `US_equity` on the model calendar, on a logarithmic scale, with the four episodes of `sim_episodes` shaded."
#| fig-asp: 0.45
sim_class_returns_monthly |>
  dplyr::filter(class == "US_equity") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(date, index)) +
  ggplot2::geom_rect(data = sim_episodes, ggplot2::aes(xmin = start, xmax = end),
                     ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, inherit.aes = FALSE,
                     fill = tidyaa_colors[["rule"]]) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = tidyaa_colors[["blue"]]) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_model() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "total-return index (log scale)")
```

The convention applies to the modeled market only. The literature keeps its
dates, and so do the real-data sleeves of @sec-02-notation-and-data-real-data.

### The class universe

The allocation spine of the book is the table `sim_class_returns_monthly`:
sixteen risky class series, five currencies (`US`, `UK`, `EU`, `CH`, `JP`) times
three classes (`government`, `credit`, `equity`) plus one global commodity
index, over `r nrow(R)` complete months, the `r max(model_year(d))` model
years, everything in US dollars and unhedged. A weekly counterpart,
`sim_class_returns_weekly`, holds the same market at the model's native
frequency, on `r dplyr::n_distinct(sim_class_returns_weekly$date)` weekly
dates.

```{r}
#| label: classes
colnames(R)
```

Five money-market series, one per region, ship beside the universe as
`sim_money_market_monthly` and are deliberately not in it. Each is the
0.25-year point on a curve fitted to that region's two, five and ten-year
yields, marked to market: a short-duration bond rather than a bill held to
maturity, and so not the risk-free rate either. One calculation settles the
point:

```{r}
#| label: money-market
M  <- as_xts_pm(sim_money_market_monthly, date, class, return)
stopifnot(all(as.Date(zoo::index(M)) == as.Date(zoo::index(R))))
mm <- as.numeric(M[, "US_money_market"])

round(c(negative_months_money_market = mean(mm < 0),
        negative_months_bill         = mean(rf < 0),
        correlation                  = stats::cor(mm, rf)), 3)
```

`US_money_market` tracks the bill at a correlation of
`r sprintf("%.2f", stats::cor(mm, rf))`, and is negative in
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(mm < 0))` of months against the bill's
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(rf < 0))`. A risk-free rate has to be riskless
over the holding period. The four foreign money markets have almost no duration
and are, unhedged in dollars, nearly pure currency positions. The money markets
are there for the chapters that need a short-duration asset or a currency
exposure; `sim_riskfree_monthly` is the risk-free rate everywhere.

@tbl-02-classes gives the three numbers a reader needs to place each series.
The return is the compounded figure of @eq-02-compounded, the Sharpe ratio
divides its excess over the bill's compounded return by the volatility, and
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation carries the full table with
skewness, kurtosis and drawdowns.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-02-classes
#| tbl-cap: "The sixteen risky class series, annualized from monthly data. Return is compounded; Sharpe is the excess of that return over the bill, divided by the volatility."
#| echo: false
region_levels <- c("US", "UK", "EU", "CH", "JP", "GLOBAL")
kind_levels   <- c("equity", "government", "credit", "commodity")

classes <- tibble::tibble(
  class  = colnames(R),
  region = factor(sub("_.*$", "", class), region_levels),
  kind   = factor(sub("^[^_]+_", "", class), kind_levels),
  ret    = apply(R, 2, ann_ret)[class],
  vol    = apply(R, 2, ann_vol)[class]
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(sharpe = (ret - ann_ret(rf)) / vol) |>
  dplyr::arrange(region, kind)
stopifnot(!anyNA(classes$region), !anyNA(classes$kind), nrow(classes) == 16L)

classes |>
  dplyr::transmute(class,
                   ret    = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ret),
                   vol    = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * vol),
                   sharpe = sprintf("%.2f", sharpe)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr", col.names = c("", "return", "volatility", "Sharpe"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-02-indices
#| fig-cap: "Total-return indices of the sixteen risky class series, in dollars, base 100 one period before the first observation, on a logarithmic scale so that equal vertical distances are equal percentage moves. One panel per asset class, one line per region."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.75
idx <- sim_class_returns_monthly |>
  dplyr::group_by(class) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rebuilt = 100 * cumprod(1 + return)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::mutate(region = factor(sub("_.*$", "", class), region_levels),
                kind   = factor(sub("^[^_]+_", "", class), kind_levels))

# The shipped index is the compounded return series, base 100 one period before
# the first observation. Assert it rather than assume it.
stopifnot(max(abs(idx$rebuilt - idx$index)) < 1e-8,
          !anyNA(idx$region), !anyNA(idx$kind))

ggplot2::ggplot(idx, ggplot2::aes(date, index, colour = region)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.45) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ kind, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_model() +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "total-return index (log scale)")
```

### How the class series are built

Each equity class is the value-weighted return of its constituent securities,
weighted on their market capitalization at the **previous** weekly observation,
never the contemporaneous one, so no portfolio is formed on information it could
not have had; the capitalizations are `sim_marketcap_weekly`, which reaches back
before model year 1 so that a prior week exists even for the first return date.
Government, credit and commodity classes are equally weighted, because no
capitalization exists for a constant-maturity bond or a commodity index. The
weekly frequency is the model's own, and a monthly class return is the
compounded weekly return within the month: every monthly date is a month end,
every week lies in the month it compounds into, and the monthly series is the
weekly-rebalanced portfolio observed at month ends, not a monthly-rebalanced
one. That can be checked rather than believed:

```{r}
#| label: monthly-from-weekly
weekly_compounded <- sim_class_returns_weekly |>
  dplyr::mutate(month = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(class, month) |>
  dplyr::summarise(compounded = prod(1 + return) - 1, .groups = "drop")

both <- sim_class_returns_monthly |>
  dplyr::mutate(month = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(weekly_compounded, by = c("class", "month"))

stopifnot(nrow(both) == nrow(sim_class_returns_monthly),
          all(both$date == lubridate::ceiling_date(both$month, "month") - 1),   # month ends
          min(sim_marketcap_weekly$date) < min(sim_class_returns_weekly$date)) # a prior week
max(abs(both$return - both$compounded))
```

### The instrument universe

Underneath the sixteen classes sit `r nrow(sim_assets)` individual instruments,
described one per row in `sim_assets` and carried at both frequencies in
`sim_asset_returns_monthly` and `sim_asset_returns_weekly`. This is the same
market at a finer grain and the universe of the sleeve chapters of Part VI:
@sec-21-equity-sleeve-theory selects within the equity block and
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory within the bonds.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-02-instruments
#| tbl-cap: "The instrument universe by region and asset class. Equities carry one of eight sectors; credit carries an investment-grade or high-yield grade."
#| echo: false
stopifnot(dplyr::n_distinct(stats::na.omit(sim_assets$sector)) == 8L,
          setequal(stats::na.omit(sim_assets$credit_grade), c("IG", "HY")))
sim_assets |>
  dplyr::count(region, asset_class) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = asset_class, values_from = n, values_fill = 0L) |>
  dplyr::mutate(region = factor(region, region_levels)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(region) |>
  dplyr::select(region, equity, government, credit, money_market, commodity) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "equity", "government", "credit", "money market", "commodity"))
```

```{r}
#| label: instrument-metadata
n_by_class <- table(sim_assets$asset_class)
c(sectors = dplyr::n_distinct(stats::na.omit(sim_assets$sector)),
  grades  = dplyr::n_distinct(stats::na.omit(sim_assets$credit_grade)))
```

The `r n_by_class[["equity"]]` equities are individual securities, each tagged
with one of `r dplyr::n_distinct(stats::na.omit(sim_assets$sector))` sectors;
the `r n_by_class[["credit"]]` credit instruments are three maturities in two
grades per region, `IG` and `HY`; the `r n_by_class[["government"]]` government
bonds are zero-coupon instruments held at constant two, five and ten-year
maturities; the `r n_by_class[["commodity"]]` commodities are a broad index and
seven sub-indices; and the `r n_by_class[["money_market"]]` money-market
instruments are the class series themselves, one per region. Identifiers are
anonymized, `US_EQU_01` and `EU_CRE_03` and so on: a region, an asset class and
a running number.

### Exchange rates, curves, capitalizations and rating changes

Three further tables let a chapter show what moved a series rather than only
its return, and a fourth carries sustainability information. `sim_fx_monthly`
and `sim_fx_weekly` hold the exchange rate of each of the four non-dollar
currencies, quoted as **dollars per unit of the local currency**, so that a
positive `fx_return` means the local currency appreciated and an unhedged
dollar investor gained. Because every series is unhedged in
dollars, a foreign holding carries its local return and its currency's move
together, and the hedged return is one subtraction away:

$$
r^{\text{hedged}}_{t} = r^{\text{unhedged}}_{t} - f_{t},
$$ {#eq-02-hedge}

with $f_t$ the matching `fx_return`. That is the whole of currency hedging as
this book implements it; whether to hedge, and how much, is the question of
@perold1988 and @campbell2010, which @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application
opens and @sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-implementation settles for the
strategic portfolio.

```{r}
#| label: hedge
fx <- sim_fx_monthly
hedged_vol <- function(series, region) {
  f <- fx[fx$region == region, ]
  stopifnot(all(f$date == as.Date(zoo::index(R))))      # same grid, same order
  u <- as.numeric(R[, series])
  c(unhedged = ann_vol(u), hedged = ann_vol(u - f$fx_return))
}
regions <- c("UK", "EU", "CH", "JP")
gov <- t(sapply(regions, function(r) hedged_vol(paste0(r, "_government"), r)))
rownames(gov) <- paste0(regions, "_government")
jp_equity <- hedged_vol("JP_equity", "JP")
round(rbind(gov, JP_equity = jp_equity), 3)
```

Hedging takes `JP_government` from
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * gov["JP_government", "unhedged"])` to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * gov["JP_government", "hedged"])` and does not lower
`JP_equity` at all, which moves from
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * jp_equity[["unhedged"]])` to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * jp_equity[["hedged"]])`;
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application explains why the two differ.

`sim_curve_weekly` holds the drivers of the bond block: for each region the
level, slope and curvature of a @nelson1987 yield curve, in the dynamic form of
@diebold2006 which @sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-implementation takes up, plus an
investment-grade and a high-yield credit spread per region, ten spreads in all.

```{r}
#| label: curve
sort(unique(sim_curve_weekly$series))
```

`sim_marketcap_weekly` holds the weekly market capitalization of the
`r n_by_class[["equity"]]` equities, which is what a capitalization-weighted
benchmark needs and what @sec-21-equity-sleeve-implementation builds one from.

`sim_esg_changes_quarterly` records changes in an ESG rating of the equities,
one row per change, dated at the quarter end:
`r nrow(sim_esg_changes_quarterly)` integer changes on
`r dplyr::n_distinct(sim_esg_changes_quarterly$asset)` of the
`r n_by_class[["equity"]]` equities, from model year
`r min(model_year(sim_esg_changes_quarterly$date))` on. The table carries
changes only and no starting level, so cumulating them gives a rating up to an
unknown constant, and the changes have no effect on the returns;
@sec-20-sustainability-implementation works with them.

### Three caveats, one departure, and a frozen version

Three properties of the market are consequences of how it is built, and a
reader should know them before modeling on it.

**Currency dominates foreign bonds.** Hedging removes on average
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(1 - gov[, "hedged"] / gov[, "unhedged"]))` of a
foreign government bond's dollar volatility, as the calculation above shows,
and a foreign money market is almost entirely currency. Only `US` and `GLOBAL`
series are free of it.

**The bond block is nearly rank-deficient at instrument level.** Three
maturities per region are priced off a three-factor curve, and the two credit
grades at each maturity share one credit factor, so some bond combinations are
near-exact replicas of others. The covariance matrix of the
`r nrow(sim_assets)` instruments is technically invertible and practically not:

```{r}
#| label: conditioning
A <- as_xts_pm(sim_asset_returns_monthly, date, asset, return)
stopifnot(ncol(A) == nrow(sim_assets), setequal(colnames(A), sim_assets$asset_id))

log10_condition <- function(X) {
  e <- eigen(stats::cov(X), symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
  log10(max(e) / min(e))
}
round(c(sixteen_classes = log10_condition(R), instruments = log10_condition(A)), 1)
```

A condition number of $10^{`r sprintf("%.1f", log10_condition(A))`}$ means that
unconstrained mean-variance at instrument level produces nonsense, which is
worth demonstrating rather than preventing, and it is why the sleeve chapters
shrink the matrix in the manner of @ledoit2004 or constrain the weights. At
class level the number is $10^{`r sprintf("%.1f", log10_condition(R))`}$ and
the problem does not exist; @sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory is about the
difference.

**Equity series are single securities.** The median annualized volatility of
the `r n_by_class[["equity"]]` names is
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * median(apply(A[, sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]], 2, ann_vol)))`,
which is realistic for one security, but a portfolio of these names diversifies
more readily than a real index would, because the names are few and their
idiosyncratic components are drawn independently of one another.

One departure from the estimated model is deliberate and is stated as a
parameter rather than hidden. Every euro-area equity carries an expected-return
overlay of **three percentage points a year**, added as a constant drift. It is
a capital-market assumption, not a measurement, and the sample says why it was
needed:

```{r}
#| label: overlay
overlay <- 0.03
eq      <- classes[classes$kind == "equity", ]
vol     <- setNames(eq$vol, eq$class)
without <- setNames(eq$ret - ifelse(eq$class == "EU_equity", overlay, 0), eq$class)
sharpe_without <- (without - ann_ret(rf)) / vol
eu      <- as.numeric(R[, "EU_equity"])
se_mean <- ann_vol(eu) / sqrt(nrow(R) / 12)     # sigma / sqrt(years)
stopifnot(overlay < se_mean,
          names(which.max(vol)) == "EU_equity",
          all(sharpe_without[c("US_equity", "UK_equity", "CH_equity")] >
                sharpe_without[["EU_equity"]]))

# The long-only tangency portfolio of chapter 9, with the overlay and without.
spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev")
tangency <- function(X) {
  extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(X, spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE))
}
Re_without <- Re
Re_without[, "EU_equity"] <- Re[, "EU_equity"] - overlay / 12
w_eu <- c(with    = tangency(Re)[["EU_equity"]],
          without = tangency(Re_without)[["EU_equity"]])
stopifnot(w_eu[["with"]] > 0.01, w_eu[["without"]] < 0.001)

round(c(return_without    = without[["EU_equity"]],
        sharpe_without    = sharpe_without[["EU_equity"]],
        cor_with_UK       = stats::cor(eu, as.numeric(R[, "UK_equity"])),
        cor_with_CH       = stats::cor(eu, as.numeric(R[, "CH_equity"])),
        tangency_with     = w_eu[["with"]],
        tangency_without  = w_eu[["without"]],
        se_of_annual_mean = se_mean,
        overlay_in_se     = overlay / se_mean), 2)
```

Without the overlay, `EU_equity` earns
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * without[["EU_equity"]])` a year at the highest
volatility of the five equity markets, a Sharpe ratio of
`r sprintf("%.2f", sharpe_without[["EU_equity"]])` where the United States,
Britain and Switzerland have
`r sprintf("%.2f", sharpe_without[["US_equity"]])`,
`r sprintf("%.2f", sharpe_without[["UK_equity"]])` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", sharpe_without[["CH_equity"]])`, and it correlates at
`r sprintf("%.2f", stats::cor(eu, as.numeric(R[, "UK_equity"])))` with Britain
and `r sprintf("%.2f", stats::cor(eu, as.numeric(R[, "CH_equity"])))` with
Switzerland. The long-only tangency portfolio of @sec-09-mean-variance-theory
then holds none of it, against
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * w_eu[["with"]])` with the overlay, and every chapter
that trades return against risk would have carried a dead column. The overlay
is
`r sprintf("%.1f", overlay / se_mean)` standard errors of the sample mean, so
within one; by the argument of @merton1980 that standard error depends only on
the span of the sample in years, and `r nrow(R) / 12` model years cannot
distinguish a three-point assumption from the measured mean. No other series
carries an overlay, and @sec-90-data-description records this one beside every
other modeling choice.

Finally, the dataset is **frozen at version 6.2.0**. The idiosyncratic
components are one draw, so a regenerated export is a different realized path
rather than an update, and the drift is uneven across moments. Regenerating it
is an event, not a refresh: every printed number in this book is pinned to
6.2.0, and the book's repository carries a script that recomputes the
load-bearing ones and names those a new export has moved. The full description
of every series, its construction, its units and its known limitations is
@sec-90-data-description.

## The Real Data Sleeves {#sec-02-notation-and-data-real-data}

The modeled market is the default because every number reproduces offline
for every reader. It cannot, by construction, support a claim about real
markets, and some chapters have to make one: @sec-21-equity-sleeve-implementation
measures factor premia on Kenneth French's portfolios, and
@sec-25-backtesting-application notes that every asset in the modeled market
survives to the end of the sample, a survivorship bias by construction that the
real sleeves do not share. For those, `tidypm` carries a
small data layer built the way @scheuch2023 build theirs, from free public
sources, with two additions: a pinned cutoff date and a manifest.

The layer begins with a registry. `pm_sources()` is a list with one entry per
sleeve, naming its source and carrying the function that fetches it. The
registry is data rather than state; calling it downloads nothing.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-02-sources
#| tbl-cap: "The sleeve registry of `pm_sources()`. A sleeve with no fetch function is declared so that the gap is visible rather than implied."
#| echo: false
src <- pm_sources()
tibble::tibble(
  sleeve      = names(src),
  source      = vapply(src, function(s) s$description, character(1)),
  implemented = vapply(src, function(s) isTRUE(s$implemented), logical(1))
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(implemented = ifelse(implemented, "yes", "not yet")) |>
  kable(align = "lll", col.names = c("sleeve", "source", "implemented"))
```

`r sum(vapply(src, function(s) isTRUE(s$implemented), logical(1)))` of the
`r length(src)` sleeves are built. Three equity sleeves and the cash sleeve come
from Kenneth French's data library, the market returns and risk-free rate
behind @fama1993; two government sleeves and an investment-grade credit sleeve
are constructed from FRED yields by pricing a constant-maturity bond, which is
the calculation @sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory sets out; and high yield is a
long-running mutual fund, because every free high-yield index history has been
withdrawn behind a rolling window. Two caveats on that last sleeve belong here
rather than in a footnote: a managed fund holding higher-quality high yield
**understates drawdowns**, the wrong direction for the one sleeve whose reason
to exist is its left tail, and its source is undocumented and could disappear,
so the cache protects a reader who has already built the panel and not one
arriving in ten years.

`pm_init()` walks the registry, downloads each implemented sleeve, joins them on
the month-end date and writes the result, together with a manifest, to a single
file in `pm_cache_dir()`, a directory in the user's R cache outside any project
and overridable through the environment variable `TIDYPM_CACHE`. It stops at a
pinned cutoff, exported as a constant so that a chapter can name it rather than
repeat a literal:

```{r}
#| label: cutoff
PM_CUTOFF
```

The cutoff is a calendar year end so that every annual table is a complete year
and no chapter carries a stub year in which the sources, which publish at
different speeds, have not all arrived. Run once, and read forever after:

```{r}
#| label: real-data-layer
#| eval: false
pm_init()                       # downloads once, writes the panel and its manifest
panel <- pm_data()              # a disk read: no network, no recomputation
pm_data(sleeves = c("us_equity", "gov_long"), from = "1990-07-01")
pm_check()                      # your build against the manifest the book was built on
```

`pm_data()` never reaches the network. If no panel has been cached it stops and
says to run `pm_init()`, because a function that silently downloads behaves
differently on a plane. The panel it returns is deliberately ragged: a sleeve
whose source starts later than the others is `NA` until it begins, and nothing
pads or fills those rows, because a filled gap is an estimate dressed as an
observation, and a covariance matrix estimated across one silently changes its
effective sample, which is the failure `as_xts_pm()` warns about in
@sec-01-setting-up-implementation.

The manifest is the honest version of reproducibility for data that is not ours
to redistribute. French and FRED both revise history, so a panel rebuilt today
need not equal the one the book's numbers were computed on. `pm_init()` records
an observation count and a hash per sleeve; `pm_check()` compares a reader's
manifest against the book's and names the sleeves that moved, rather than
leaving the difference to surface as an unexplained mismatch three chapters
later. No downloaded file is committed to the book's repository, and
@sec-93-package-notes records the version of every package the pipeline depends
on.

## Asset Class Vocabulary {#sec-02-notation-and-data-vocabulary}

The data uses one set of names and the industry another, and both appear in
this book. @tbl-02-vocabulary maps one onto the other. The rule is that **code
uses the data's names**, because a column is called what it is called, and
**prose uses whichever is clearer**, which is usually the industry's.

| In the data | In the industry | Note |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `government` | sovereign bonds; Treasuries, gilts, Bunds, JGBs | zero-coupon, constant two, five and ten-year maturities |
| `credit` | corporate bonds; investment grade and high yield | the same maturities in two grades, `IG` and `HY` |
| `money_market` | cash; money market | **not cash and not the risk-free rate**: a marked-to-market three-month instrument, beside the universe, not in it |
| `commodity` | alternatives; real assets | the only alternative asset in this market, one global class |
| `equity` | stocks; equities | value-weighted class of individual securities |
| `US`, `UK`, `EU`, `CH`, `JP` | United States, United Kingdom, euro area, Switzerland, Japan | the five currencies; everything is converted to dollars |
| `GLOBAL` | global | the commodity class, and the only region code without a currency of its own |
| `sim_riskfree_*` | the risk-free rate; the bill | a three-month Treasury bill, an input to the model |

: What the data calls a series and what the industry calls it. {#tbl-02-vocabulary}

One word in the table deserves a sentence. *Alternatives* usually covers real
estate, hedge funds, private equity and commodities together; this market
carries only the last, so the word appears only where the industry's usage is
being quoted.

The class level of @tbl-02-classes is where Parts III to V of the book work, and
it is the level at which the allocation literature since @brinson1986 locates
most of the variation in a diversified portfolio's return; the instrument level
of @tbl-02-instruments belongs to Part VI. Which of the two an allocation is set
at is a question of granularity. Whether it is set from long-run assumptions or
from conditioning information is a different question, that of horizon, and the
words for its two answers, *strategic* and *tactical*, are defined in
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory rather than here.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- Vectors are bold lower case, matrices bold capitals, estimates carry hats.
  $\boldsymbol{R}$ is the $T \times N$ matrix of simple total returns,
  $\boldsymbol{w}$ the weights, $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ the
  moments of **excess** returns, and @eq-02-moments gives the portfolio's mean
  and variance. Excess over the bill is the default basis everywhere; chapter 3
  says why.
- Arithmetic annualizing, mean $\times 12$ and volatility $\times\sqrt{12}$, is
  for anything that enters an optimizer. The compounded return of
  @eq-02-compounded is for what a series earned. Per period, the gap is half
  the variance.
- The modeled market contains no real data, so no series is the history of a
  real security, and it runs on model years `r min(model_year(d))` to
  `r max(model_year(d))`. `model_year()`, `in_episode()`, `fmt_model()` and
  `scale_x_model()` are how every chapter reads a date, and the four stress
  episodes are the rows of `sim_episodes`.
- The market is sixteen risky class series over `r nrow(R)` months,
  five currencies times government, credit and equity plus a global commodity
  index, all in dollars and unhedged, with `r nrow(sim_assets)` instruments
  beneath them. The five money markets ship beside the universe and are neither
  cash nor the risk-free rate; the bill is.
- Currency dominates foreign bonds, the bond block is nearly rank-deficient at
  instrument level, and equities are single names. Euro-area equity carries a
  deliberate three-point overlay, within one standard error of its sample mean.
  The dataset is frozen at version 6.2.0 because regenerating it redraws the
  idiosyncratic components.
- Real data enters through `pm_sources()`, `pm_init()`, `pm_data()` and
  `pm_check()`: a registry, one download to a cache with a pinned cutoff, an
  offline read, and a manifest that names the sleeves that have moved since the
  book was built. It is used where a claim has to be about real markets.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Apply @eq-02-hedge to all twelve non-US series in `R`, using
   `sim_fx_monthly`, and tabulate the unhedged and hedged annualized volatility
   with the share of variance the hedge removes. Group the result by asset
   class. Why does hedging remove most of a bond's volatility and almost none
   of an equity market's, and what does that say about treating currency as
   one decision per country?
2. Rebuild `GLOBAL_commodity` at weekly frequency as the equally weighted mean
   of its eight instruments in `sim_asset_returns_weekly`, then compound to
   months and compare with `sim_class_returns_monthly`. How close do
   you get, and what does the answer tell you about how the non-equity classes
   are constructed?
3. Rebuild `US_equity` at weekly frequency two ways: equally weighted across its
   instruments, and value-weighted on the previous week's capitalization from
   `sim_marketcap_weekly`. Confirm that the second reproduces the shipped
   series, then compare the annualized return and the correlation of the two.
   Which one should a benchmark use, and why does the choice move the return
   by as much as it does?
